source.text: כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אֵ֣י זֶ֠ה סֵ֣פֶר כְּרִית֤וּת אִמְּכֶם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שִׁלַּחְתִּ֔יהָ א֚וֹ מִ֣י מִנּוֹשַׁ֔י אֲשֶׁר־מָכַ֥רְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם ל֑וֹ הֵ֤ן בַּעֲוֺנֹֽתֵיכֶם֙ נִמְכַּרְתֶּ֔ם וּבְפִשְׁעֵיכֶ֖ם שֻׁלְּחָ֥ה אִמְּכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh: Where [is] this document of divorce of your mother, whom I sent her away? Or who of my creditors [is it] to whom I sold you to him? Here! For your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Where [is] the certificate of divorce of your mother, whom I sent away? Or which of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} creditors [is it] to whom I sold you? Look, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Where is the certificate of divorce I gave your mother when I sent her away? Or to which of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} creditors did I hand you over in payment? No, it was for your own guilt that you were sold, and for your rebellions that your mother was sent away.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Did I divorce your mother? If I did, where is the paper that proves it? Did I sell you to pay off a debt? Who did I owe money to? No! You were sold because of your sins. Your mother was sent away because you turned against me.

decisions.choice: certificate of divorce: the written document a husband gave his wife when he ended the marriage
decisions.reason: The law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4 required a written certificate when a man sent his wife away. Zion is the mother and her people the children; God asks for the document and there is none. The exile was not a final, legal end to the marriage (compare Jeremiah 3:8, where Israel is given such a certificate, and 54:6-7).

decisions.choice: which of my creditors: a father in debt could sell his children to pay what he owed
decisions.reason: Children could be taken or sold to settle a debt (Exodus 21:7; 2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5). God owes no one; the question expects the answer that he never sold his people out of need.

decisions.choice: for your iniquities you were sold: the exile came from the people's own sins, not from God's weakness or debts
decisions.reason: The verse answers both questions. God did not reject Zion without cause or give her children away; the exile was the result of their guilt and rebellion (42:24; 43:27-28).

decisions.choice: guilt / sins; rebellions / turned against me
decisions.reason: The two nouns are the usual words for iniquity and transgression. Balanced uses "guilt" and "rebellions"; Readable says "sins" and turns the second into a plain statement.

decisions.choice: Did I divorce your mother? If I did, where is the paper that proves it? Did I sell you to pay off a debt?
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what the two questions imply: God is asking whether he ever ended the marriage or sold his children for debt.

source.text: מַדּ֨וּעַ בָּ֜אתִי וְאֵ֣ין אִ֗ישׁ קָרָֽאתִי֮וְאֵ֣ין עוֹנֶה֒ הֲקָצ֨וֹר קָצְרָ֤ה יָדִי֙ מִפְּד֔וּת וְאִם־אֵֽין־בִּ֥י כֹ֖חַ לְהַצִּ֑יל הֵ֣ן בְּגַעֲרָתִ֞י אַחֲרִ֣יב יָ֗ם אָשִׂ֤ים נְהָרוֹת֙ מִדְבָּ֔ר תִּבְאַ֤שׁ דְּגָתָם֙ מֵאֵ֣ין מַ֔יִם וְתָמֹ֖ת בַּצָּמָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Why did I come and there [was] not anyone? [Why] did I call and there [was] not [one] answering? Really, is it short, is my hand short from ransom? Or [is there] not in me strength to deliver? Here! By my rebuke I dry up [the] sea; I make rivers a wilderness; their fish stink because there [is] not water, and die by thirst.

en.L: Why, when I came, [was there] no one? [Why], when I called, [was there] no one answering? Is {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand really too short to ransom? Or [is there] no strength in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to deliver? Look, by {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} rebuke I dry up the sea; I make rivers a wilderness; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst.
en.B: When I came, why was no one there? When I called, why did no one reply? Is {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand so short that it cannot ransom, or do I lack the power to rescue? With a single rebuke I drain the sea dry and turn rivers into wasteland. Their fish rot where the water has gone, and they perish from thirst.
en.R: I came to you, but no one was there. I called, but no one answered. Do you think I am too weak to save you? Do you think I do not have the power to rescue you? I only have to speak a sharp word, and the sea dries up. I can turn rivers into desert. Then the fish rot because there is no water, and they die of thirst.

decisions.choice: is my hand too short: am I too weak?
decisions.reason: A short hand is one that cannot reach far enough to help; the same picture is used in 59:1 and Numbers 11:23. The answer the question expects is no.

decisions.choice: ransom, deliver: to free by paying a price, and to snatch out of danger
decisions.reason: The first word belongs to buying back a slave or a firstborn (Exodus 13:13; Deuteronomy 7:8). It fits verse 1: God can buy his children back from any creditor.

decisions.choice: I dry up the sea; their fish stink: the power shown at the exodus
decisions.reason: God's rebuke drying the sea recalls the crossing of the sea (Exodus 14:21; Psalm 106:9), and the stinking fish recall the first plague on the Nile (Exodus 7:18, 21).

decisions.choice: Do you think I am too weak to save you?
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the short hand and frames the questions as God's challenge to the people.

source.text: אַלְבִּ֥ישׁ שָׁמַ֖יִם קַדְר֑וּת וְשַׂ֖ק אָשִׂ֥ים כְּסוּתָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: I clothe [the] heavens [with] darkness, and sackcloth I make their covering.

en.L: I clothe the heavens [with] blackness, and sackcloth I make their covering.
en.B: I dress the skies in black and wrap them in sackcloth like a cloak.
en.R: I can make the sky turn dark, as if it were dressed in black clothes for a funeral.

decisions.choice: blackness and sackcloth: the dress of mourning
decisions.reason: Mourners wore sackcloth, a rough dark cloth of goat hair (15:3; 22:12). The sky itself is pictured as dressed for grief. The darkness may also recall the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exodus 10:21-23).

decisions.choice: as if it were dressed in black clothes for a funeral
decisions.reason: Readable explains sackcloth as mourning dress rather than naming it.

source.text: אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהֹוִ֗ה נָ֤תַן לִי֙ לְשׁ֣וֹן לִמּוּדִ֔ים לָדַ֛עַת לָע֥וּת אֶת־יָעֵ֖ף דָּבָ֑ר יָעִ֣יר׀בַּבֹּ֣קֶר בַּבֹּ֗קֶר יָעִ֥יר לִי֙ אֹ֔זֶן לִשְׁמֹ֖עַ כַּלִּמּוּדִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] Lord Yahweh has given to me a tongue of taught [ones], to know to help the weary [with] a word; he awakens in [the] morning, in [the] morning he awakens my ear to hear like taught [ones].

en.L: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has given me a tongue of those taught, to know [how] to sustain the weary [with] a word. He wakes [me] morning by morning; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wakes my ear to hear as those [who are] taught.
en.B: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has given me the tongue of one who is taught, so that I know how to bear up the weary with a word. Each morning {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rouses me; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rouses my ear to listen as a learner listens.
en.R: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has taught me what to say, so that I can give strength to people who are tired and discouraged. Every morning {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wakes me up and makes me ready to listen, like a student listening to a teacher.

decisions.choice: me: the servant of the LORD speaks, though he is not named until verse 10
decisions.reason: Verses 4-9 are the third of the servant passages (42:1-4; 49:1-6; 52:13-53:12). In 41:8 the servant is Israel the people (see the note there), but here the servant speaks as one person, listens where Israel would not (42:18-20; 48:8), and suffers for it. Verse 10 calls him "his servant". The Gospels show Jesus suffering in the way these verses describe (Matthew 26:67; 27:30).

decisions.choice: tongue of those taught: the speech of a disciple, who says what he has learned
decisions.reason: The word means people who are taught, disciples (8:16; 54:13). It comes twice: the servant speaks as one taught and listens as one taught. What he says comes from what God tells him each morning.

decisions.choice: to sustain: to help or hold up
decisions.reason: This verb is found only here, and its meaning is guessed from the context and from related words. "Help" or "sustain" fits the weary as its object.

decisions.choice: has taught me what to say; makes me ready to listen, like a student
decisions.reason: Readable explains "tongue of those taught" and "wakes my ear" in plain words.

source.text: אֲדֹנָ֤י יְהוִה֙ פָּתַֽח־לִ֣י אֹ֔זֶן וְאָנֹכִ֖י לֹ֣א מָרִ֑יתִי אָח֖וֹר לֹ֥א נְסוּגֹֽתִי׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] Lord Yahweh has opened my ear, and I not I have been rebellious; backward not I have turned.

en.L: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has opened my ear, and I, I was not rebellious; I did not turn backward.
en.B: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has opened my ear, and I have not resisted; I have not turned away and gone back.
en.R: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} has helped me to listen, and I have not refused to obey. I have not turned away from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: opened my ear: made me hear and understand, so that I obey
decisions.reason: To open the ear is to reveal something to a person (Job 36:10; Psalm 40:7). Unlike the people whose ear was not opened (48:8), the servant hears and obeys.

decisions.choice: and I, I was not rebellious: the pronoun is stressed
decisions.reason: The added "I" sets the servant against the rebellious people (1:20; 30:9). He did not resist what he was told, though it led to the suffering of verse 6.

decisions.choice: I have not turned away from him
decisions.reason: Readable says who the servant did not turn from.

source.text: גֵּוִי֙ נָתַ֣תִּי לְמַכִּ֔ים וּלְחָיַ֖י לְמֹֽרְטִ֑ים פָּנַי֙ לֹ֣א הִסְתַּ֔רְתִּי מִכְּלִמּ֖וֹת וָרֹֽק׃

records.literal_gloss: My back I gave to strikers, and my cheeks to pluckers; my face not I hid from insults and spit.

en.L: My back I gave to [those who] strike, and my cheeks to [those who] pluck [the beard]; my face I did not hide from insults and spitting.
en.B: I let those who struck me have my back, and those who tore at my beard have my cheeks. I did not turn my face away from insult and spit.
en.R: People beat my back, and I let them. They pulled out the hair of my beard, and I did not stop them. They insulted me and spat on me, and I did not hide my face.

decisions.choice: those who pluck: men tearing out the hair of the beard
decisions.reason: The verb means to make bare by pulling out hair (Ezra 9:3; Nehemiah 13:25). Tearing a man's beard was a deep public shame (2 Samuel 10:4-5).

decisions.choice: I gave, I did not hide: the servant accepts the suffering willingly
decisions.reason: The servant does not run from his attackers; he offers his back and face. The Gospels tell how Jesus was struck and spat on (Matthew 26:67; 27:30; Mark 14:65).

decisions.choice: I let those who struck me have my back
decisions.reason: Hebrew puts "my back" first for stress. Balanced and Readable put the attackers first so that the sentence reads naturally.

source.text: וַאדֹנָ֤י יְהוִה֙ יַֽעֲזָר־לִ֔י עַל־כֵּ֖ן לֹ֣א נִכְלָ֑מְתִּי עַל־כֵּ֞ן שַׂ֤מְתִּי פָנַי֙ כַּֽחַלָּמִ֔ישׁ וָאֵדַ֖ע כִּי־לֹ֥א אֵבֽוֹשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] Lord Yahweh helps me; therefore not I have been humiliated; therefore I have made my face like flint, and I know that not I will be put to shame.

en.L: And the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} helps me; therefore I have not been humiliated; therefore I have made my face like flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame.
en.B: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} is my help, so disgrace has not overcome me. That is why I have made my face like flint, and I know I will not be put to shame.
en.R: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} helps me, so I will not let their insults defeat me. I have made up my mind, and nothing will change it. I know I will not be shamed.

decisions.choice: I have made my face like flint: I am set and will not turn back
decisions.reason: Flint is the hardest common stone (Ezekiel 3:8-9, where God makes the prophet's forehead hard). The servant faces his opponents with a fixed purpose. Luke 9:51 says Jesus "set his face" to go to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: not humiliated, not put to shame: the insults do not break him, and God will clear him in the end
decisions.reason: The first verb looks at the present: the insults of verse 6 have not crushed him. The second looks to the outcome: God will not let him be shamed (verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: I have made up my mind, and nothing will change it
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the face like flint.

source.text: קָרוֹב֙ מַצְדִּיקִ֔י מִֽי־יָרִ֥יב אִתִּ֖י נַ֣עַמְדָה יָּ֑חַד מִֽי־בַ֥עַל מִשְׁפָּטִ֖י יִגַּ֥שׁ אֵלָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Near [is] the [one] justifying me; who will contend with me? Let us stand together; who [is] the master of my case? Let him draw near to me.

en.L: Near [is the one who] declares me in the right; who will contend with me? Let us stand together; who [is] the owner of my case? Let him come near to me.
en.B: The one who will declare me in the right is close at hand. Who will take me to court? Let us stand up side by side. Who has a case against me? Let him step forward and face me.
en.R: God is near, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will show that I am innocent. So who will accuse me? Let us go to court together! Who wants to bring a charge against me? Let him come and face me!

decisions.choice: the one who declares me in the right: God, as judge, acquits the servant
decisions.reason: The verb is the courtroom word for declaring someone innocent (5:23; Deuteronomy 25:1). Paul echoes verses 8-9 in Romans 8:33-34: God is the one who justifies; who will condemn?

decisions.choice: the owner of my case: my opponent at law
decisions.reason: The phrase is literally "the master of my judgment", the one who brings the case against me. The servant challenges any accuser to stand up with him before the judge.

decisions.choice: God is near, and he will show that I am innocent
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who declares the servant in the right, as verse 9 does.

source.text: הֵ֣ן אֲדֹנָ֤י יְהוִה֙ יַֽעֲזָר־לִ֔י מִי־ה֖וּא יַרְשִׁיעֵ֑נִי הֵ֤ן כֻּלָּם֙ כַּבֶּ֣גֶד יִבְל֔וּ עָ֖שׁ יֹאכְלֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Here! [The] Lord Yahweh helps me; who [is] he [who] will condemn me? Here! All of them like a garment will wear out; a moth will eat them.

en.L: Look, the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} helps me; who [is] he [who] will condemn me? Look, all of them will wear out like a garment; [the] moth will eat them.
en.B: Yes, the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} stands by me; who then can pronounce me guilty? All of them will fall apart like worn-out clothes, and the moth will devour them.
en.R: The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} is helping me. So who can say I am guilty? All my enemies will fall apart like old clothes. They will be like cloth eaten by moths.

decisions.choice: condemn: declare guilty in court
decisions.reason: The verb is the opposite of "declare in the right" in verse 8. With God as his helper and judge, no accuser can win against the servant.

decisions.choice: wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them: his accusers will not last
decisions.reason: Old clothing and moth-eaten cloth picture what wastes away (51:6, 8; Job 13:28; Psalm 102:27).

source.text: מִ֤י בָכֶם֙ יְרֵ֣א יְהוָ֔ה שֹׁמֵ֖עַ בְּק֣וֹל עַבְדּ֑וֹ אֲשֶׁ֣ר׀הָלַ֣ךְ חֲשֵׁכִ֗ים וְאֵ֥ין נֹ֨גַהּ֙ ל֔וֹ יִבְטַח֙ בְּשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה וְיִשָּׁעֵ֖ן בֵּאלֹהָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Who among you fears Yahweh, listens to the voice of his servant? Who has walked [in] darkness, and there [is] not brightness for him, let him trust in the name of Yahweh and let him depend on his God.

en.L: Who among you fears {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, [who] listens to the voice of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servant? [Whoever] has walked [in] darkness and has no light, let him trust in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and lean on his God.
en.B: Who among you fears {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and listens to the voice of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servant? Let the one who walks in darkness, with no glimmer of light, trust in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and lean on his God.
en.R: Do any of you respect {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? Do you listen to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servant? Then even if you are walking in the dark and cannot see any light, trust in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Depend on your God.

decisions.choice: who has walked in darkness: the faithful listener who has no light, told to trust God
alternatives: the servant, who walked in darkness
decisions.reason: The clause can describe the servant (he walked in darkness, yet trusted) or the hearer who follows him. Taken with the call to trust, it most likely speaks to the hearer: whoever obeys the servant and is still in the dark should rely on God, as the servant did (verses 7-9).

decisions.choice: his servant: the LORD's servant, the one who spoke in verses 4-9
decisions.reason: The speaker of verses 4-9 is named here as the LORD's servant. Fearing the LORD and obeying his servant go together.

decisions.choice: respect the LORD; trust in the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable says "respect" for the reverent fear meant here and "trust in the LORD" for trusting in his name, since the name stands for the person.

source.text: הֵ֧ן כֻּלְּכֶ֛ם קֹ֥דְחֵי אֵ֖שׁ מְאַזְּרֵ֣י זִיק֑וֹת לְכ֣וּ׀בְּא֣וּר אֶשְׁכֶ֗ם וּבְזִיקוֹת֙ בִּֽעַרְתֶּ֔ם מִיָּדִי֙ הָיְתָה־זֹּ֣את לָכֶ֔ם לְמַעֲצֵבָ֖ה תִּשְׁכָּבֽוּן׃פ

records.literal_gloss: Here! All of you kindling a fire, girding on firebrands, walk in the flame of your fire and in firebrands you have kindled; from my hand this will be to you: in pain you will lie down.

en.L: Look, all of you who kindle a fire, who arm yourselves with firebrands: walk in the flame of your fire and among the firebrands you have kindled! From {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand this will be [given] to you: in torment you will lie down.
en.B: But all of you who light a fire and arm yourselves with blazing torches, go on, walk by the glare of your own fire, among the torches you have set alight! This is what you will receive from {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand: you will lie down in agony.
en.R: But some of you are lighting your own fires. You carry burning torches to light your own way. Go ahead and walk by the light of your own fire and your torches! But this is what I will do to you: you will lie down in great pain.

decisions.choice: kindle a fire, arm yourselves with firebrands: those who make their own light instead of trusting God
alternatives: those who set fires to harm others
decisions.reason: Verse 10 told the one in darkness to trust the LORD. These people light their own fires instead. The fire may also be meant as a weapon against the servant; either way it turns back on them.

decisions.choice: from my hand: the LORD himself speaks and gives the punishment
decisions.reason: The servant spoke in verses 4-9, but the one who hands out the outcome here is God, as in verses 1-3. The servant does not judge in his own name.

decisions.choice: you will lie down in torment: you will end in pain
decisions.reason: Lying down is going to sleep, or to death (14:18; 43:17). The word for torment means grief or pain (Psalm 16:4).

decisions.choice: to light your own way
decisions.reason: Readable states what the fires are for, in light of verse 10. This follows m1; the other reading (fires to harm others) is not chosen at any level.
